analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security benefits for low earners, caregivers, and seniors, funded by taxes on high incomes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2024 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died without a hearing, markup, or vote when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits across the board: a richer benefit formula, a minimum benefit tied to the poverty line for long-time low earners, unpaid caregiving years counted as earnings, an inflation index built for seniors, a 5% bonus at age 82 (or after 20 years on benefits), and no five-month waiting period for disability or survivor benefits. It would pay for this with payroll taxes on a share of wages above the Social Security cap and by raising the net investment income tax on high-income investors from 3.8% to 6.8%, sending 44.1% of that revenue to the Social Security trust fund. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries would gain: lifetime low earners (a minimum benefit rising up to 125% of the poverty line with 30+ years of work), unpaid family caregivers of young children or chronically dependent relatives (up to 60 months of care credited as wages worth 50–100% of the national average wage), disabled workers and surviving spouses (the five-month waiting period eliminated), and all beneficiaries (the first benefit bracket paid at 95% instead of 90%, an elderly-specific inflation index for annual cost-of-living raises, and a 5% increase at age 82 or 240 benefit months). People on SSI, Medicaid, or CHIP would be held harmless so bigger Social Security checks don't cost them other aid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-earning seniors, unpaid caregivers, disabled workers

how_it_helps.text: A richer benefit formula for everyone: the first bracket of average earnings is paid at 95% instead of 90%, and the second bracket grows one percentage point a year starting in 2030 until it is 15% higher in 2044.

A real anti-poverty floor: beneficiaries with 11 to 30+ years of work get a minimum benefit scaling up to 125% of the annual poverty guideline, benefiting lifetime low earners, with existing beneficiaries' amounts recomputed.

Caregiving counts: up to 80 hours a month of unpaid care for a child under 16 or a chronically dependent relative is credited as deemed wages of 50% to 100% of the national average wage, with at most the last 60 qualifying months counted.
Cost-of-living raises would use a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers reflecting retiree spending, and beneficiaries would get a 5% increase at age 82 or after 240 benefit months.

The five-month waiting period for disability insurance benefits and for surviving-spouse benefits is eliminated for applications filed after enactment, and SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries are held harmless.

The bill's own stated funding: payroll taxes apply to 80% of wages above the annual cap in 2025 (stepping down to 0% by 2029), and the net investment income tax rises from 3.8% to 6.8% starting in 2025, with 44.1% of it dedicated to the Social Security trust fund.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and their employers would pay payroll tax on 80% of wages above the Social Security cap in 2025, with that share stepping down each year to zero in 2029. High-income investors would pay a net investment income tax raised from 3.8% to 6.8% starting in 2025 — a 3-point surcharge on capital gains, dividends, and other investment income above existing thresholds — with 44.1% of the proceeds routed to the Social Security retirement trust fund.

drawbacks.text: The ongoing financing is thin on its face: the payroll tax on wages above the cap steps down to zero in 2029, so every permanent benefit expansion would ride on the higher investment-income tax alone, and the text offers no demonstration that the program is actually 'stronger for future generations' as the title claims.

High earners get a sweetener alongside the taxes: after 2029, wages above the cap are untaxed for Social Security yet 5% of those 'surplus' earnings still count toward a larger benefit, a provision paid for by the investment surtax that raises fair questions from any side.

The timing tilts against current workers: the across-the-board formula increases, the age-82 bonus, and the surplus-earnings credit apply only to people newly eligible after 2029, while the taxes start in 2025 — so today's near-retirees mostly see the costs, not the benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concrete and large for poor seniors, unpaid caregivers, and disability applicants, and the taxes fall almost entirely on the top of the income scale — the design points the money in the right direction. The honest caveat is the arithmetic: with the above-cap wage tax expiring in 2029, the bill's permanent benefit expansions depend on the higher investment-income tax, and nothing in the text proves that covers the cost; a serious version of this bill would need independent actuarial certification. As it happened, no one had to weigh any of this, because the bill never advanced past its referral day.

outcome.mechanism: It died in committee: referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never taken up again before the 118th Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill on September 11, 2024, in the final session months of the 118th Congress; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
No senator from either party ever cosponsored it — the cosponsor list stayed at zero.

The committee held no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and the Senate never considered it on the floor; the action history ends with the September 11, 2024 referral before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and investors are better off because the bill never advanced — no new payroll taxes above the cap and no higher investment-income tax ever took effect. Current and future beneficiaries gained nothing: no higher minimum benefit, no caregiver credit, no richer formula.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 11, 2024; it was his alone — no cosponsor ever joined.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in his committee from its referral day until the Congress ended.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; the chamber never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: One Democrat introduced the bill, zero senators of either party cosponsored it, and no vote ever happened, so no partisan split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill's funding comes almost entirely from them: payroll taxes on 80% of wages above the Social Security cap in 2025 (stepping down to zero by 2029) and a net investment income tax raised from 3.8% to 6.8% from 2025, with 44.1% of that revenue dedicated to Social Security. The bill's death spared them every one of those taxes.

industries.industry: Fund managers and professionals paid in investment income
industries.note: People whose pay is largely investment income, such as carried interest, would owe the higher 6.8% surtax; in partial exchange, their earnings above the cap would count toward a larger Social Security benefit through the surplus-earnings provision.
